extracted.intended_audience: tax attorneys, corporate counsel for pharmaceutical/generic manufacturers, patent litigators, and accountants advising on tax treatment of litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Judicial guidance on whether Hatch-Waxman (Section 271(e)) litigation expenses incurred by ANDA filers must be deducted as ordinary and necessary business expenses or capitalized under the Internal Revenue Code and implementing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 162 — ordinary and necessary business expenses (deductibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: 26 U.S.C. § 162(a) authorizes taxpayers to deduct 'ordinary and necessary expenses paid or incurred during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an expenditure qualifies as an 'ordinary and necessary' business expense under Section 162, it is deductible in the year incurred rather than capitalized and amortized. The practical tax effect is immediate cost recovery versus multi-year amortization for capital items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 263 — prohibition on deducting capital expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: 26 U.S.C. § 263(a) prohibits deductions for 'capital expenditures' (costs incurred in the acquisition or disposition of a capital asset), and capital assets include property with a useful life substantially beyond the taxable year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a payment is a capital expenditure, it must be capitalized (depreciated or amortized) rather than deducted. Capital assets may be tangible or intangible (see 26 U.S.C. § 263(c)). The rule substantially affects timing of cost recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 161 precedence — when payment qualifies as both deduction and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: If a particular payment might qualify both as an ordinary and necessary expense (deductible) and as a capital expenditure, the Tax Code requires that Section 263 take precedence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In that circumstance the payment must be treated as a capital expenditure and not deducted. See 26 U.S.C. § 161 and Commissioner v. Idaho Power Co., 418 U.S. 1 (1974).

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of the claim test (Woodward/Gilmore)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 'origin of the claim' doctrine, the controlling inquiry is whether the origin and character of the claim litigated is in the process of acquisition of a capital asset; if the origin is capital in nature, the expenditure is not deductible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key corollaries: the taxpayer's motive is irrelevant; the consequences (possible effects on taxpayer's fortunes) are irrelevant; focus on the nature of the proceeding itself, but avoid a purely formalistic inquiry that ignores how the litigation fits into a larger transaction. Applied to Hatch-Waxman litigation, the Court concluded the origin is a patent infringement claim (patentee's suit), not acquisition of FDA approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: INDOPCO 'significant future benefit' test
rubrics_metrics.description: INDOPCO (503 U.S. 79) articulates that expenditures providing a significant future benefit to the business may require capitalization rather than immediate deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard looks to whether the expenditure creates or enhances an asset that yields future benefits; the IRS regulations (26 C.F.R. § 1.263(a)-4) were issued to implement this approach for intangibles.

rubrics_metrics.name: 26 C.F.R. § 1.263(a)-4 — payments to create or to facilitate creation of intangibles (regulatory test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation requires capitalization of '[a]n amount paid to create an intangible' and of '[a]n amount paid to facilitate . . . an acquisition or creation of an intangible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation defines 'facilitate' broadly as 'the process of investigating or otherwise pursuing the transaction' and defines 'transaction' as 'all of the factual elements comprising an acquisition or creation of an intangible' and can include a 'series of steps carried out as part of a single plan.' Application asks whether the expense 'facilitates' acquisition/creation of the intangible (i.e., is part of the transaction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step approach (origin-of-claim then application of §1.263(a)-4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-step test (used by the Court of Federal Claims and described in the opinion) first applies the origin-of-the-claim doctrine to ascertain the character and nature of the expenditures, then applies the capitalization-of-intangibles regulations (C.F.R. § 1.263(a)-4) to that ascertained character to determine whether capitalization is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hybrid approach focuses first on the nature of the litigation (what claim is being litigated) and then asks whether, given that nature, the expenses fall within regulatory categories requiring capitalization (e.g., amounts paid to facilitate creation of an intangible). The Federal Circuit noted it need not decide the correctness of the hybrid approach because the outcome was the same under either test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether litigation 'facilitates' acquisition — necessary-precondition rule (regulatory examples, e.g., Example 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the litigation is a necessary precondition to acquiring the asset (i.e., the litigation must be resolved to complete the acquisition), then the litigation 'facilitates' the acquisition and expenses are capital expenditures (as in Example 10/American Stores where antitrust litigation threatened a merger).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory examples distinguish litigation that blocks or is essential to the transaction (capitalizable) from litigation that is separate from the acquisition process. Example 10 (antitrust regulator litigation) is analogous where regulatory or litigation outcomes prevent the acquisition itself; by contrast, litigation that merely runs in parallel but is not required to complete the transaction does not facilitate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing/delay alone does not establish 'facilitate' (litigation that only delays effective approval)
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation that can delay the timing of when an asset's benefits become effective, but that does not determine whether the asset is acquired, does not 'facilitate' the acquisition for purposes of §1.263(a)-4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to Hatch-Waxman: district-court litigation can delay effective FDA approval (e.g., automatic 30-month stay), but only the FDA can grant final approval; because the litigation does not grant or is not a precondition to approval, it does not facilitate acquisition of the intangible (FDA approval) and thus is not capitalizable on that ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature-of-proceeding focus — disregard taxpayer motive or consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis must focus on 'the nature of the proceeding itself' (the origin/character of the claim litigated), not on the taxpayer's motive for incurring the expense or the potential consequences of litigating for the taxpayer's assets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations: Woodward and Gilmore. Practically, even if a litigant defends to obtain a regulatory benefit, the relevant question is whether the litigation itself is part of the acquisition chain; motivations and downstream effects are not controlling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity principle for patent litigation — defense costs generally deductible
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses incurred defending against ordinary patent infringement claims are generally deductible on the theory that the taxpayer is protecting or maintaining its income-generating business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because §271(e) Hatch-Waxman suits are litigated in essentially the same manner as ordinary patent infringement suits, the Court relied on the established deduction treatment in ordinary patent litigation to support deductibility for ANDA filers defending §271(e) claims; imposing different tax treatment on the opposing parties in the same litigation would be incongruous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application-specific criterion for Hatch-Waxman disputes — origin is patentee's §271(e) claim, not ANDA approval
rubrics_metrics.description: For ANDA filers facing Hatch-Waxman suits, the origin of the litigation expense is the NDA holder's patent infringement claim (Section 271(e) Claim) rather than the ANDA filer's pursuit of FDA approval; thus such expenses are not incurred 'in the process of acquisition' of an FDA approval asset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court's applied reasoning: FDA review and patent litigation are distinct 'lanes,' resolved by different decisionmakers; the litigation may affect timing (e.g., 30-month stay) but does not control FDA's substantive approval decision, so the litigation does not constitute facilitation or acquisition of the FDA-approved intangible and therefore is deductible.
